newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao scores legal gains.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao scores legal gains.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao won three small but symbolically important victories on Friday as courts upheld his claims for special treatment in criminal cases clouding his political future.
The Supreme Court ordered that two trials involving the former prime minister should be moved from a crowded local court to a more secure, isolated location.
Rao has been charged in a seven-year-old forgery case. He has also been summoned to appear in court in a 13-year-old case of criminal conspiracy to cheat.

Rao, who has round-the-clock bodyguards with machineguns, and Delhi police had argued he could be attacked by extremists if he appeared at the sprawling Tis Hazari court, where two trial hearings were planned for next week.

An appearance by Rao at the Tis Hazari court, which handles even petty offences, could have proved an embarrassment for the former prime minister, who rarely ventures outside his heavily-guarded New Delhi home.

Rao, who resigned as prime minister in May after his Congress party suffered a humiliating defeat in general elections, stepped down as Congress party chief last month after being summoned to appear in court in the cheating case.

He has retained considerable clout in Congress as the head of the party's parliamentary delegation. His party provides make-or-break support in parliament to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition.
The Supreme Court ordered Delhi police to propose a safer location by next Monday.

Authorities have suggested Rao be tried in a spacious, marble-lined conference hall on a tree-lined street, a venue which is more easily protected than Tis Hazari and considered more in keeping with the stature of a former prime minister.
In another potentially important decision, the Supreme Court ruled that the special commando bodyguards who surround Rao night and day must be provided at all times.

The Special Protection Group (SPG) of black uniformed commandos was formed to protect the prime minister in 1988, four years after prime minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by Sikh bodyguards during a Sikh separatist revolt in Punjab.

Her son, Rajiv Gandhi, was killed in May 1991, about six months after he resigned as prime minister. Parliament then extended SPG protection to ex-prime ministers, who are covered for 10 years after leaving office, and their families.
Delhi court authorities had said Rao's SPG protective cover would have to be lifted once he entered a local court.
But the Supreme Court said the special cover "goes with the person of the protectee as the shadow would a man".

Court authorities said the ruling that special cover could not be lifted greatly diminished the chances Rao, pending the completion of trial, would be put in custody in Tihar jail. Instead, he would now probably be kept at home, they said.
Two others accused in the cheating case are currently in custody in Tihar, Asia's biggest prison.
In a third ruling, a local judge exempted Rao from appearing at a hearing in the forgery case set for next Monday.
On Wednesday, Rao was briefly arrested at home, then freed on bail in the forgery case. He has been charged with using forged documents to try to defame a rival politician in 1989.
